newsitem.title: USA: Fischler sees 'compromise' on modified-gene labels.
newsitem.headline: Fischler sees 'compromise' on modified-gene labels.

text.p: A European Union proposal that would require the labeling of food products containing "genetically-modified" soybeans and other farm goods will likely be changed before it goes into effect, a top E.U. official said Monday.

"In the end, I think we will reach a kind of compromise" on the issue, E.U. Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler commented after a speech outlining the need for further E.U. agricultural policy reform.

Fischler was in town Monday for talks with U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, as well as the chairmen of the House and Senate Agriculture Committees.
Late last week, a group of 29 U.S. farm and trade organizations wrote Glickman to express concern about the labeling proposal being advanced by Fischler.

If implemented, Fischler's plan "would result in major market disruptions, high price discounts to U.S farmers and could potentially disrupt access for U.S. agricultural exports to the E.U.," the group said.

Fischler's proposal would require labeling of all raw materials and products containing "genetically-modified organisms" (GMOs) imported into and processed in the E.U. It would also mandate that GMO crops and products be kept separate throughout the marketing system.
In his remarks Monday, Fischler said it would be a "very big mistake" for Europe to ignore advances in biotechology, such as GMOs, that promise to substantially increase food production.
But many European consumers, especially in German-speaking countries, are opposed to genetically-modified food products. "What can we do in such a situation?," he said.
Fischler pledged that the E.U. would honor its committment under the Uruguay Round trade pact to base food safety standards on sound science, rather than consumer preferences.
But consumers still deserve to know whether food products contain GMOs so they can make a choice, he said.
